routes.label: Follow the units from meters to skips

question: Suppose hops, skips and jumps are specific units of length. If \(b\) hops equals \(c\) skips, \(d\) jumps equals \(e\) hops, and \(f\) jumps equals \(g\) meters, then one meter equals how many skips?
solution:
Assume first that the stated conversions use nonzero amounts, as usual in a unit-conversion problem. In particular, \(b,d,g\ne0\), so the following divisions are valid.

From \(f\) jumps equaling \(g\) meters, one meter equals \(f/g\) jumps. From \(d\) jumps equaling \(e\) hops, each jump equals \(e/d\) hops. Finally, each hop equals \(c/b\) skips. Following this chain gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
1\text{ meter}
&=\frac fg\text{ jumps}\\
&=\frac{ef}{dg}\text{ hops}\\
&=\frac{cef}{bdg}\text{ skips}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the answer under the nonzero conversion assumption is \(\frac{cef}{bdg}\) skips, choice \(\mathrm{D}\).

The displayed statement does not explicitly impose that assumption. If \(b=c=d=e=f=g=0\), every given equality simply says that zero length equals zero length. A skip could then be one meter long or half a meter long, giving respectively one or two skips per meter while satisfying every displayed equality. Consequently, the literal statement permits no unique answer; choice \(\mathrm{D}\) requires the usual nonzero conversion interpretation.
